title: The good, the bad, and the vague in the new college accreditation rule
summary: The Education Department’s final accreditation rule boosts campus speech protections in some places and invites trouble in others.
full_text:
Last week, the Department of Education finalized new regulations governing federally recognized accrediting organizations. These private agencies serve as quality-assurance gatekeepers for more than $100 billion in annual federal student aid, making their standards deeply influential over institutional policy. The department’s new regulations could therefore substantially alter institutional policies, including free expression policies.

Historically, federal regulations have left accreditors with substantial freedom to set their own standards and have had little to say regarding free speech or academic freedom (though most accreditors have voluntarily incorporated these principles into their standards). But more recently, accreditors have come under scrutiny for failing to exercise proper oversight of their accredited colleges, including claims that they fail to enforce their standards for free speech and academic freedom. FIRE’s own experience lends credence to these claims. On several occasions, we have contacted accreditors to report an institution’s noncompliance with the accreditor’s academic freedom or free expression standards. Unfortunately, our complaints have usually been rejected or ignored, with little to no explanation.

The regulations change the equation by establishing more detailed expectations concerning faculty policies, academic freedom, free expression, and intellectual diversity—in some ways for better and in some ways for worse. FIRE submitted a formal comment to the department in September, offering support for provisions that bolstered campus expressive rights and suggestions to address vague or overbroad language. Here’s what advocates for free expression need to know about the substance of the final rule. (The regulations also address many issues unrelated to FIRE’s mission, which are not addressed here or in our comment.)

Bad: making accreditors interpret religious doctrine

The regulations exempt religious institutions from certain academic freedom and viewpoint diversity requirements. However, they subsequently require accreditors to evaluate whether a religious institution’s academic freedom and viewpoint diversity policies are “consistent with the institution’s religious mission.” Essentially, this appears to task accreditors with determining whether a religious institution is properly implementing its own religious doctrine regarding academic freedom and viewpoint diversity.

If applied in this manner, this provision would run afoul of the First Amendment, which protects the right of churches and other religious institutions, including religious universities, to decide matters “of faith and doctrine” without government intrusion.

When police treat free speech as suspicious activity

Police monitoring of public meetings risks chilling free speech. When protected expression becomes suspicious activity, everyone has reason to worry.

Read More

Courts have frequently rejected regulations on this basis. For example, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit applied this doctrine to a higher education regulatory scheme in Colorado. It explained that government scrutiny of whether a religiously affiliated university’s “stated commitment to academic freedom could be squared with [its] statement of religious beliefs” would present an “intrusion into religious affairs.” Similarly, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit criticized the National Labor Relations Board for using a religious school’s academic freedom commitment as evidence of certain employees’ nonreligious status. This move, the court said, “impermissibly sided with a particular view of religious functions.” The court criticized the Board’s refusal “to accept that faculty members might contribute to a school’s religious mission by exercising their academic freedom, even though many religious schools understand the work of their faculty to be religious in just this way.”

The Education Department argues that the regulation does not require religious institutions “to adopt viewpoint-range, intellectual-diversity policies, or academic-freedom protections that would conflict with” their religious mission. However, the text of the rule leaves that determination to accreditors acting on behalf of the government. Ultimately, then, this provision poses a serious threat to the First Amendment rights of religious institutions.

Academic freedom and the First Amendment

Good: Protecting constitutional academic freedom

Section 602.17(a)(2)(iii) of the final rule requires accreditors to evaluate whether nonreligious institutions maintain academic freedom protections that are “clearly articulated and applied consistently to faculty regardless of . . . viewpoint, or ideology.”

As applied to public institutions, this is a worthy requirement. Public universities are constitutionally prohibited from retaliating against faculty on the basis of their viewpoints, and accreditors should ensure that taxpayer dollars are not going to institutions that flout their constitutional obligations.

Bad: restricting institutional autonomy at private universities

The provision is more complicated as applied to private institutions. Many private colleges voluntarily promise robust academic freedom, and FIRE has long urged both institutions and accreditors to take those commitments seriously. If the Education Department’s rule simply required accreditors to ensure that private universities live up to their stated promises, it would be a strong addition. Instead, this provision effectively requires every secular private institution to maintain viewpoint-neutral academic freedom protections.

That’s a meaningful distinction. Private institutions possess expressive and associational interests protected by the First Amendment. Some private colleges exercise these rights by organizing around particular academic or philosophical missions, and so may choose to retain authority to ensure that faculty activity remains consistent with the institution’s stated mission. A federal funding condition that functionally eliminates this discretion raises serious First Amendment concerns.

The department argues that this language is process-oriented and that an institution’s decision not to adopt a formal policy on academic freedom does not, by itself, constitute noncompliance. But the lack of clarity in the regulatory text itself leaves room for confusion and potential abuse.

Good: striking the right balance with the First Amendment

Another provision in the same section, (a)(2)(v), takes the right approach regarding First Amendment protections more broadly. It requires accreditors evaluating public institutions to consider whether they maintain “consistently applied policies that protect the First Amendment” while instructing them to “similarly evaluate” private institutions that voluntarily guarantee “the same or similar” protections. (Confusingly, later language in this same section, (a)(2)(vii)(c), seems to take this approach with respect to academic freedom, but the new regulations do not reconcile this section with the language previously discussed.)

Vague: evaluating whether institutions “appropriately prioritize” intellectual diversity

Section 602.17(a)(2)(viii) requires accreditors to evaluate whether nonreligious institutions have “a policy that is designed to support, promote, and appropriately prioritize intellectual diversity and the free exchange of ideas amongst faculty, to include elements that address intellectual inquiry and student learning, and measures student and faculty perceptions on the range of viewpoints and perspectives offered by the institution or program.”

As FIRE has long argued, intellectual diversity, understood as meaningful exposure to competing ideas, arguments, methods, and schools of thought, is a real educational good. A university cannot truly fulfill its mission if students and faculty are deterred from challenging prevailing views, testing controversial hypotheses, or debating contested questions. But incorporating undefined language about viewpoint diversity into federal regulations carries real risk. What does it actually mean for an institution to “appropriately prioritize” intellectual diversity? It’s anybody’s guess, and some accreditors and institutions may overread the provision to require particular levels of ideological representation.

Student journalists know their rights. Universities should too.

Student journalists know their First Amendment rights. Universities must do more to protect those rights, not stand in the way of their reporting.

Read More

The Education Department said that it does not intend to prescribe institutional policies or override institutional autonomy. But without any of the clarifying language we suggested in our comment, the regulations could be misinterpreted in ways that do precisely that.

Good: preventing accreditors from abusing their authority

Two provisions in the new regulations will help limit the ways in which accreditors can wield their authority to threaten institutions’ First Amendment rights and obligations.

First, Section 602.18(b)(4) requires nonreligious accreditors to ensure that decisions “are neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology that are unrelated to its accrediting policies or standards.” This language is helpful. Accreditors are quality-assurance bodies, and their decisions should not turn on their approval or disapproval of an institution’s political or ideological orientation.

Second, Section 602.15(f) provides that an agency’s accreditation standards “must not restrict public institutions from fulfilling their obligations under the First Amendment,” nor may they restrict private institutions that “guarantee the same or similar protections.” This is a strong addition. The government should ensure that accreditors are not wielding their authority to prevent public institutions from complying with core constitutional obligations. Similarly, although private universities are not state actors subject to the First Amendment, they are free to adopt these standards in order to ensure robust, wide-open campus debate. The government — and gatekeepers to federal funds — should welcome this decision, not stand in its way.

Vague: a poorly worded religious carveout

Unfortunately, this provision also includes a poorly worded carveout for religious institutions. It states that an accreditor may not restrict a private institution from guaranteeing First Amendment protections “unless the institution has a religious mission.” The way this is written, it appears to say that an accreditor can require a religious university to restrict speech, even if it doesn’t want to. The Education Department explains that this language is intended to preserve institutional autonomy — but as written, it does the exact opposite.

Good: clarifying complaint procedures

The final rule bolsters the mechanisms through which students, faculty, and staff may communicate accreditation concerns directly to accrediting agencies. In our comment, we recommended that the department explicitly state what current regulations seem to require: that accreditors must review third-party complaints regarding institutional compliance (e.g., complaints from watchdog groups like FIRE). Although the department ultimately declined to incorporate the suggestion, it nevertheless acknowledged in its explanation that accreditors should review third-party complaints and provided instructions on what to do when an accreditor fails to provide such review, stating:

If an entity submits a complaint to an agency and does not believe that it has been sufficiently vetted, then the entity can submit a complaint to the Department for review of the agency’s response to aslrecordsmanager@ed.gov or call 202-453-7615. The commenters may also attend a NACIQI [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity] meeting and provide public comment regarding an accrediting agency.

An open question

Some have argued that several of the provisions in the new regulations are barred by federal law. They point to 20 U.S.C. § 1099b(o), which requires the secretary to establish regulations for recognizing accreditors but specifically prohibits “promulgat[ing] any regulation with respect to” certain accreditation standards, including “faculty.” But despite this provision, and as discussed above, the final rule describes what an accrediting agency must evaluate when applying its standards regarding faculty.

In response to this plausible statutory prohibition, the Education Department argued that subsection (o) means “the secretary may establish recognition criteria governing whether an accrediting agency functions as a reliable authority under Section 496, while leaving to accrediting agencies the responsibility for developing and applying their own substantive accreditation standards.” Because FIRE’s chief focus lies in academic freedom and free speech, our analysis has focused on the substance of the proposed regulations and does not take a side.

Conclusion

We welcome the Education Department’s renewed attention to the role that academic freedom, freedom of expression, and open inquiry play in educational quality. Accreditors should not pressure public institutions to violate the First Amendment, prevent private institutions from honoring speech protections they voluntarily adopt, or make accreditation decisions based on ideological favoritism. The final rule makes meaningful progress on each of those fronts. Additionally, the rule will help ensure that accreditors monitor public universities for compliance with core First Amendment obligations. At the same time, other provisions are sufficiently vague to be abused or seriously threaten constitutionally protected institutional autonomy — especially at religious institutions.

FIRE stands ready to work with institutions and accreditors trying to comply with the rule in a manner that protects and bolsters freedom of inquiry and freedom of expression on campus.

title: Student journalists know their rights. Universities should too.
summary: Student journalists know their First Amendment rights. Universities must do more to protect those rights, not stand in the way of their reporting.
full_text:
On Oct. 17, the Maryland Terrapins squandered a double-digit halftime lead against Rutgers — marking their fifth straight defeat of the season, at home, on homecoming. Four days later, the university announced head football coach Mike Locksley would be leaving.

Nolan Rogalski and Jude Wilkenfeld, managing editor and deputy editor of the student-run Testudo Times, headed to the team’s practice facility to get players’ reactions after they received a tip about a players’ meeting. But then a UMD Athletics staff member called the cops.

Rogalski later posted on X: “Wilkenfeld and I were outside Jones-Hill House trying to get players to comment. An athletics staffer took pictures of us, and a police dispatch was called for suspicious activity; a cop and 2 cop cars pulled up, and officers ID’d us and asked us to leave.”

“We certainly didn’t mean to cause any trouble,” Rogalski says in the video he posted, “But as far as we were aware, we were standing in places we were allowed to stand.”

“I don’t disagree with you,” replies the officer.

Wilkenfeld said the staffer had never asked who he or Rogalski were, nor did they ask if they were student journalists.

“If the staffer had asked us who we were and what we were doing, the whole situation could have been avoided entirely,” Wilkenfeld told FIRE.

The Testudo Times later reposted Rogalski’s video along with an official statement from the University of Maryland’s Police Department and Maryland Athletics. “Due to heightened concerns for staff and player safety around the football program in recent weeks,” the statement said, “there has been increased security around athletics facilities. A UMPD officer approached the two individuals, learned they were with a campus media organization, recorded student IDs, and no report was taken.”

It added, “UMPD and Maryland Athletics respect the First Amendment rights of all journalists reporting in public spaces.”

Since the incident, UMD is making good on that statement. The UMD Athletics Department has agreed to meet with FIRE’s Student Press Freedom Initiative to make sure students and staff alike are on the same page when it comes to their free speech rights. It’s a step in the right direction, and one FIRE would love to see from more universities across the country.

Student journalists shouldn’t always have to fight to use their protected rights.

The Supreme Court has held that a college campus has “many of the characteristics of a public forum.” A large, open quad, for instance, has the same basic look and function of a city park. Sidewalks, like the one on which these student journalists stood, are also considered traditional public forums. As such, students — including student journalists — have the right to freely express themselves in these public spaces.

Luckily, Rogalski and Wilkenfeld knew their rights and stood up for themselves. Like other student journalists, they couldn’t simply rely on government officials to defend their rights, or even properly understand what they might be. Just last week, Cat Murphy — a student at UMD’s graduate school for journalism — had to stand her ground when U.S. Rep. Andy Harris falsely claimed that Maryland law required her to get his permission before recording him (that rule only covers private conversations). Harris even told his security to take her phone and get police to escort her out.

The paper was her lifeboat — UMD called it interference

She founded a Muslim student paper for community. Now UMD calls her reporting on a protest “interference” — and is pursuing discipline.

Read More

UMD students aren’t the only ones who have had to stand up for their rights in the field over the past few months. Dylan Hembrough, editor-in-chief of the independent student paper The Alestle at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, was reported to police by a university communications official when he simply tried to assert his and his campus newspaper’s right to free expression. An SIUE administrator stopped a reporter for The Alestle from interviewing staff without her present. In an email, Hembrough called out the university’s marketing and communications team for interfering with the student outlet’s newsgathering process, at which point the administrator reported Hembrough’s email as harassment. (It was not.) Hembrough has vocally defended his right to report, and SPFI’s case with SIUE remains ongoing.

Courts have held time and time again that universities have an obligation to maintain, among other constitutional rights, a free student press. As Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart wrote in Shelton v. Tucker: “The vigilant protection of constitutional freedoms is nowhere more vital than in the community of American schools.” It’s also important for universities to adequately articulate to faculty and staff what that maintenance looks like to protect the free, open “marketplace of ideas” college campuses are meant to be. Policies and practices safeguarding students’ right to free expression need to be fully articulated to all faculty and staff, and they should have support to uphold and follow through on those safeguards.

Among those safeguards must be a way to prevent students from self-censorship to avoid punishment or other retribution, keeping what’s called the “chilling effect” at bay. When authorities are called to investigate students standing on a sidewalk, that negatively affects student journalists’ ability to gather news and exercise their First Amendment rights and bolsters the chill. Not only does the call rattle student journalists in the moment, but it dissuades other student journalists in the future from using their own free expression to engage in reporting that benefits the whole community.

It’s great to see student journalists assert their rights. But public universities must also help by upholding their First Amendment obligations. Student journalists shouldn’t always have to fight to use their protected rights, and universities should cultivate an environment where student journalists feel comfortable enough to exercise those rights without fear of censorship, retaliation, or challenge.

title: ‘People are active, they are fed up’: young voters fueled the Democratic wave
summary:
After helping Trump to victory in 2024, young voters swung decisively toward Democrats, helping deliver a wave of midterm victories

The 2026 blue tsunami owes a lot to the youth vote.

According to data from Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (Circle), which monitors youth civic engagement, early estimates show the second-highest youth turnout in a midterm election in 30 years, second only to 2018, when an estimated 31% of young voters turned out during Donald Trump’s first presidency.

full_text:
The 2026 blue tsunami owes a lot to the youth vote.

According to data from Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (Circle), which monitors youth civic engagement, early estimates show the second-highest youth turnout in a midterm election in 30 years, second only to 2018, when an estimated 31% of young voters turned out during Donald Trump’s first presidency.

While voters over 45 were roughly split between parties, voters ages 18-29 went for congressional Democrats at a 35-point edge, across race, gender, ethnicity, and education levels. Latino youth went for Trump by slim majorities in 2024; this year, they voted Democrat by margins of +10 to +15. 63% of young white men went for Trump in 2024; this cycle, 54% voted Dem. White young women also switched allegiance from 2024 by +15. Rural voters went from 50% voting for Trump in 2024 to 60% supporting Democratic candidates.

This is something of a return to form for the youth vote, which leaned Democratic by double digits in elections between 2018 and 2022. Indeed, the +35 lean for voters 18-35 parallels that in the 2018 blue wave which elected populist Democrats like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, said Leela Strong, the director of Circle.

“It was such a soundbite for 2024, about the shift of young white men specifically, and folks without formal college experience,” said Strong. “Now, even though we’re comparing a midterm to a presidential, we’re seeing shifts among those demographic groups switching back to Democrats, overwhelmingly so.”

According to Strong, the data even suggests that 15% of young people who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate this cycle. The outcome has been so decisive that Republicans are openly fretting over heavily Blue youth vote turnout in states like Florida, Georgia and South Carolina.

In battleground states – Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Nevada, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin – the estimated youth turnout was, in aggregate, 30%.

“I voted because in my working-class, immigrant neighborhood, families are afraid to go outside, drive to work or pick up their kid from school,” said Motyko Morales, 26, an artist in Miami, who says her family members have experienced “real physical and psychological impact” over attacks on legal routes to citizenship and the threat of third-country deportations. She’s “cautiously optimistic” that congressional Democrats will “hold ICE accountable and reverse course on harmful legislation”.

“For the first time in my life, I got to see a candidate that looked [like] and represented the same values of the Rio Grande Valley that I have,” said Amanda Chapa, 22, a recent college graduate and community organizer from Rio Grande City, Texas, of Gina Hinojosa. The governor-elect won 77% of voters 18-29, based on exit polling analysis from NBC News. In 2024, Trump flipped Starr county on the Texas-Mexico border – where Rio Grande City is located – by over 70 points; this year, despite navigating barriers to the polls, voters flipped it back by over 70 points.

Just over half of young voters ranked the economy and jobs as their top priority, followed by healthcare, Iran, immigration, education and the climate. Chapa’s top issues were reinstating cut funding to Medicaid and fighting ICE and the “brutalization of our community members”.

Sarah John, 26, a law student from Los Angeles, said she’s critical of Democrats, but having witnessed the impacts of Trump’s ICE raids in LA (still being felt), she strongly believed her vote against Republicans would make a difference. On Thursday, Los Angeles elected its first democratic socialist mayor, Nithya Raman – making two of the country’s three biggest cities now run by democratic socialists.

The enthusiasm even reached states without competitive federal races. Patrick Schranck, 27, who manages an independent movie theater in Portland, “identif[ies] more as an independent these days” and is active in his local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapter. He spent Tuesday night at Portland DSA’s election night party celebrating the re-election of their three city councilmembers.

Schranck remains skeptical of congressional Democrats’ ability to “fix everything” with their newfound majorities, but, he said: “I’m just glad to see the Republicans lose and see more socialists and progressives get elected nationally.”

For Jordan Korgood, 24, of Boston, voting in this election was especially personal. The Massachusetts sexual health educator feels so passionately about civic engagement that she filed to run for a state board seat overseeing judicial appointments. But another candidate in the primary had Korgood tossed from the race on a technicality: Because she was homeless for a few months while in college in 2023, her opponent argued she could not meet the five-year residency requirement.

“Voting was the most immediate and direct way I could still engage with electoral politics in a meaningful way,” said Korgood, whose biggest issues were protecting the first amendment and trans rights. Regardless of who was up for re-election in Massachusetts, she said it felt necessary “at a time when fascists who seek to limit or repress my rights as a trans woman are seated in office in both red states and blue states alike”.

Young people were credited in part with powering Trump’s 2024 win, though just under half of eligible young voters turned out, not hitting the 50% turnout achieved in 2020. Plenty chose to sit out the election over US funding for Israel’s assault in Gaza, as well as the decision by both schools and elected officials to criminalize students in the thousands for protesting it. They also felt that the Democratic party had failed to offer a strong counter to what Republicans had on offer, instead tacking to the center.

In a sign of things to come, a year later, 75% of New York City voters 18-29 chose democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani as the city’s mayor, forming “his strongest supporter [bloc] out of all age groups” in the election tally, according to Circle. Political commentators and national party leaders argued a DSA campaign like his could only win in New York City.

Twenty-six-year-old Elise Joshi runs the progressive campus program More Perfect University and has spent the last several months hosting many of the progressive candidates that won big Tuesday at “Students vs. Billionaires Town Halls” on college campuses across the country. When the program launched this spring, Joshi told the New York Times that it was intended in part as a progressive counterpoint to Turning Point USA, whose existing campus presence has expanded in the year since Charlie Kirk’s killing. She argued that TPUSA “refus[es] to champion working-class issues”, and that youth voters were desperate for candidates who would.

Candidates like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed – whose campaign slogan was “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for All,” and who refused to compromise on trans girls in sports – are at the forefront of what Joshi and others are calling a blue tsunami.

“We’ve been in Florida, Maine, North Carolina, and I’ve seen the youth enthusiasm every single time – and not just enthusiasm for a specific candidate: Students who are very inquisitive about the issues and the solutions to those issues they’re dealing with, [from] from healthcare to economic issues to trans rights,” said Joshi. “Young people are active, they are fed up with corporate greed and corruption from Washington, and are ready to be really engaged in politics in all the ways you can be.”

More than a few of the successful candidates promising change, regardless of location, are young people themselves, like Melat Kiros, 29, the newly elected Colorado congresswoman who defeated a 15-term incumbent; many are DSA candidates. This week, Providence, Rhode Island, elected its youngest-ever mayor: 28-year-old David Morales, a democratic socialist. That same day, the city became the largest in the United States to vote in support of divesting from “companies complicit in genocide”, organized by the Providence for Palestine campaign.

In a period of global youth uprising against government corruption and seizing power in elections, it’s a partial answer to anyone questioning when America might see its youth in revolt. It’s also a rebuke to a tremendous amount of Republican campaign spending. Elon Musk alone spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republicans and attacking candidates like Texas’s James Talarico, especially on trans issues. Talarico went on to win voters ages 18-29 by nearly 50 points.

“With the price of gas what it is alongside a hiring freeze, the only solution offered by the Republican party was to blind yourself with bigotry and pick a God and pray – except it has to be the Christian one, or else,” said model Vivian Wilson, 22, who has been financially independent from Musk, her father, since she came out as trans as a teenager. “Spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ‘trans kids boogieman’ ads makes voters feel like they’re being talked down to or ignored – which they were – rather than focusing on any actual tangible policy for change.”

She sees youth turnout for Democrats as only logical amid economic crisis, war on Iran, military support for Israel, ICE raids, and “the known sexual misconduct of Republican candidates”.

Wilson added: “There have been so many nails placed in this coffin that it’s turning into a Theseus’ ship kind of situation.”

“We feel fantastic,” said Kidus Girma, campaigns director for the Sunrise Movement, the youth climate organization that burst on to the scene in 2018 with a sit-in for the Green New Deal in then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office alongside newly elected Ocasio-Cortez. This week, one of the movement’s cofounders, Will Lawrence, 36, won his race in Michigan, with Sunrise’s support.

Joshi and Girma are clear: It’s not “vote blue, no matter who.” There are plenty of power players still in the party who organizers feel didn’t listen to them outside election years, when they need them to power youth turnout.

Up next: Holding these new electeds – and the Democratic party – accountable. On Thursday, Wilson posted to her Instagram account backing a rising call from the US young left to reject Senator Chuck Schumer and congressman Hakeem Jeffries for leadership positions in the new Congress. By Saturday, a Change.org petition calling for Jeffries’ leadership ouster had attracted more than a million signatures.

This article was amended on 7 November 2026. An earlier version said Jordan Korgood’s bid for a state board seat in Massachusetts ended after an intervention by the 41-year-old incumbent. In fact, it was another candidate who intervened.

title: Melania Trump and LSU announce a scholarship program for students who were in foster care
summary: Trump and LSU secured more than $7 million in private donations to create an endowment fund for the scholarships, the White House said.
full_text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Melania Trump on Saturday announced a multimillion dollar partnership between Louisiana State University and her "Fostering the Future" program to provide scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system.

"This achievement will give young people from foster care an anchor of stability, a strong educational foundation and a chance to build a wonderful life," she said at an event with LSU President Wade Rousse.

Trump and LSU secured more than $7 million in private donations to create an endowment fund for the scholarships, the White House said. MMR Group Inc., an electrical contracting company based in Baton Rouge, committed $5 million, with additional LSU Foundation donors providing more than $2 million, the White House said.

The first lady later planned to attend the football game between LSU and Alabama, which also is participating in the initiative.

"As adults, we have a moral obligation to our children, especially those in foster care. But, as you know, we must act to truly make a difference. The foster care community doesn't need words," she added, before concluding her brief remarks by saying, "Now, let's go and enjoy the game."

There are 14 scholars under the program at LSU and nine at Alabama, she said, part of a group of 100 students supported across 26 schools this semester.

The foster care program was being featured across the campus as well as on the field at Tiger Stadium just before kickoff, the White House said.

WATCH: First lady Melania Trump announces Fostering the Future partnership with IndyCar and Fox

Rousse presented her with an LSU helmet with the "Be Best" logo and an LSU jersey with the "Be Best" patch that he said every player would wear in the game. The broader "Fostering the Future" initiative is an offshoot of the "Be Best" campaign that was her signature issue during President Donald Trump's first term.

"At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said. "That is why access is one of our highest priorities. Students who have experienced foster care have already demonstrated resilience, determination and potential. Our responsibility, our responsibility is to make sure circumstances beyond their control do not stand between them and a life-changing higher educational experience."

The first lady started working on foster care issues after the Republican president's first term ended in 2021, and created "Fostering the Future" to provide resources and support, including scholarships. LSU is among more than 20 colleges and universities nationwide that participate in the program.

Earlier this year, Melania Trump was on Capitol Hill to push Congress to pass a legislative package that would broaden access to services for young people in foster care by updating a decades-old program. The measures cleared the House and are pending in the Senate.

WATCH: First lady Melania Trump announces new investment accounts for foster youth

During the appearance, she told members of the House Ways and Means Committee that young people in foster care face barriers to housing, transportation and other challenges outside of the classroom that affect their performance in school along with their future financial independence.

"We can close this gap," she said in April. "New legislation for the foster care community is a moral imperative."

Last November, the first lady spearheaded an executive order signed by the president linking the federal government, colleges and universities, the private sector and charitable groups to create educational and employment opportunities for those in foster care.

She also created "Fostering the Future Together," a global version of the program with more than 45 participating countries.

Alabama and LSU, meanwhile, are historical regional rivals and both teams entered the week in contention for a College Football Playoff berth. Thousands of people, many of them tailgating before the game, filmed the first lady's motorcade as it drove through campus.

Donald Trump has attended two prior LSU games as president: one at Alabama in 2019 and one in New Orleans in January 2020, when LSU defeated Clemson for the national championship. Melania Trump accompanied him to the second game.

The president was not scheduled to attend Saturday's game.

AP Sports Writer Brett Martel in Baton Rouge, La., contributed to this report.
